Triggers.value: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents' is a hard-to-explain trigger because it implies a transport/accident trauma context rather than disaster-related cues. This is not just unusual; it mismatches the stated trauma type and is not supported by the other selected items.

issues.item: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The Threat node includes 'Flashbacks', which is more a re-experiencing/memory phenomenon than a current threat belief or arousal cue. Given that Memory is structurally isolated in the formulation, placing a prominent memory-like item in Threat creates a formulation mismatch, especially when no Memory items are endorsed to support that link.

The trigger pattern is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster. 'Being seen' and 'feeling watched or observed' imply an interpersonal/social-threat cue set rather than reminders of an impersonal disaster. With no memory items or appraisals referencing social judgment, persecution, or assault, these two trigger items look clinically mismatched to the trauma context.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: The negative appraisals 'I am inadequate' and 'I can't rely on myself' can occur after trauma, but in this profile they pair mainly with social-observation triggers and do not connect clearly to a natural-disaster formulation. The remaining items emphasize generalized threat/hypervigilance, whereas these appraisals suggest a more interpersonal/shame-based presentation. That makes the profile as a whole less coherent.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'feeling watched or observed' is difficult to reconcile as a trauma-linked trigger. It suggests interpersonal persecution/surveillance rather than an environmental disaster cue, while the other trigger items are disaster-congruent.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: 'Scanning exits' is not impossible, but paired with a natural-disaster trauma and the other selected items it points toward man-made/interpersonal danger in enclosed spaces rather than the presented disaster context. This makes the threat profile feel partially mismatched to the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate
issues.explanation: The negative-appraisal set is otherwise about global damage and reduced self-reliance after trauma. 'I am inadequate' can occur in PTSD, but here it reads as a generalized self-worth theme without a clear link to the disaster-based trigger/threat pattern, making the appraisal node somewhat less coherent than the other two items.

vignette:
Amara had always been defined by her precision and control, qualities that had propelled her from her home in Nigeria through an accelerated medical program and into a coveted surgical residency at the age of twenty-one. Six months ago, that sense of control had been violently washed away. She was driving home from a 36-hour shift during a torrential thunderstorm when the road ahead disappeared under a sudden surge of dark water. Her car stalled, then lifted, tossed by a current that slammed it against a concrete barrier. For what felt like hours, she was trapped in the pitch black, the car groaning under the pressure of the floodwaters, the only sounds the relentless pounding of the rain and the shriek of the wind. She had felt a profound, paralyzing helplessness, certain she was going to die alone in the dark.

In the weeks that followed, Amara insisted she was fine, throwing herself back into the grueling pace of her residency. She believed she could wall off the memory, treating it like a clinical problem to be managed. But the trauma refused to stay contained. The first sign was the sound. A metal tray of instruments clattering to the tile floor in the operating room made her flinch so violently she nearly dropped her scalpel. The ordinary sounds of the city at night-a car backfiring, a distant siren-now sent a jolt of pure adrenaline through her, leaving her breathless and trembling. She became intensely watchful, her eyes constantly scanning the exits in every room, her phone's home screen a permanent display of the weather radar. She had come to believe that disaster was always imminent, and that only through constant vigilance could she hope to survive it.

The strategies she developed to cope began to shrink her world. She had once relied on long-distance running to clear her head, but she gave it up entirely. The feeling of her own heart pounding in her chest during exercise was now indistinguishable from the terror she felt in the flooded car, and she couldn't bear it. At the hospital, she worked tirelessly to project an image of unshakable calm, pouring all her energy into suppressing any flicker of emotion. This constant effort left her feeling brittle and disconnected. Last month, when a senior attending sharply criticized her technique, she didn't defend herself or explain her reasoning. Instead, a wave of fear washed over her, and she found herself becoming excessively compliant, nodding and apologising in a way that felt utterly foreign to her character, desperate to de-escalate a threat that existed only in her own nervous system.

The rain is her worst tormentor now. Any approaching storm sends her into a state of quiet panic. Her heart races, a cold sweat breaks on her skin, and she feels an overwhelming urge to flee, though she has nowhere to go. At night, she often wakes up in the absolute dark of her bedroom, disoriented and gasping, the memory of being trapped returning with suffocating clarity. In these moments, her hard-won identity as a capable, decisive surgeon feels like a lie. She is convinced she can no longer rely on her own judgment or her body's responses. The belief that her life has been irrevocably damaged has taken root, a quiet certainty that the bright future she worked so tirelessly to build has been destroyed. After the incident with the attending, she realized her tightly controlled world was collapsing. The fear of making a fatal error in the OR, of her unravelling becoming visible to everyone, finally outweighed the fear of admitting she needed help. She arrived at her first appointment consumed by a single, terrifying thought: that she was fundamentally broken and could never be put back together again.
